papers.title: Auditing Chatbots for Incursion into Professional Legal Practice
papers.abstract: The provision of legal advice has long been in the exclusive jurisdiction of licensed attorneys-a boundary that unauthorized practice of law (UPL) doctrine maintains to protect the public from incompetent counsel. We argue that this boundary is being redrawn, not by courts or bar authorities, but by frontier AI companies. While early chat models were trained to avoid dispensing legal advice, modern models have been reconfigured to reduce refusals and prioritize helpfulness. We ask whether chatbots increasingly do tasks that require a law degree and bar admission, and whether this is harmful in high-stakes legal domains. We develop UPLBench, a benchmark derived from court decisions finding UPL in high-stakes legal domains (e.g., immigration, family law). We then audit 23 chatbot models dating from 2023 to present, evaluating whether chatbots refuse or provide substantive legal advice, and whether they refer users to lawyers or legal aid. Unlike prior work that aims to establish the legal capabilities of chatbots (e.g., bar exam performance), our approach converts legal doctrine into a testable benchmark for evaluating chatbot adherence to law. We find modern chatbots increasingly perform tasks courts reserve for lawyers and decreasingly recommend that users consult lawyers. Subject matter expert attorneys reviewing our transcripts identified interaction patterns, such as failure to elicit relevant facts, that would be considered inadequate counsel. If acted upon, such advice could lead to deportations, loss of homes, and family separations-the very harms that UPL rules are designed to protect against. We weigh paths forward to protect the public, including compelling models to comply with existing law. We call upon the legal profession to respond to this incursion into its domain of expertise as there are insufficient protections and remedies for users who rely on chatbot legal advice.

papers.title: DOCKET: A Pluralistic Benchmark for Evaluating AI-Assisted Policy Feedback in U.S. Rulemaking
papers.abstract: As AI models advance and impact deliberative democracies, there is a growing need to assess their support of pluralistic viewpoints. Most pluralism benchmarks are insufficient for this: they are not grounded in diversity (i.e., stakeholders across different frames, skills and needs), quality (i.e., rigorous and technical debates), and impact (i.e., invested deliberators and real-world outcomes). To address this, we first (i) curate DOCKET, the most comprehensive dataset of the U.S. Federal Notice & Comment process to date. DOCKET consists of 42.3M public comments on 22,400 regulations across 44 government agencies between 2016 and 2026 and contains millions of policy debates; we link public comments to particular policy items proposed by regulators to track the public's attention and the responsiveness of regulators to public input. (ii) Next, we demonstrate the pluralistic utility of DOCKET - we show that public commenters have a wide breadth of perspectives with significant depth in policy expertise and that regulators are often responsive. (iii) Finally, we present DOCKETBench, the first systematic evaluation of LLMs' ability to represent human policy perspectives in federal rulemaking. Only 18-30% of LLM-generated feedback aligns with real human comments. LLMs critique proposals broadly but generally, lacking the specific grounding, citations, and lived-experience arguments that humans bring to bear; in addition, most models we test systematically agree with government perspectives (overlapping with up to 68% of their claims) and agree least with labor unions (as little as 26% of their claims), demonstrating a fundamental skew in perspectives that even tools like persona modeling do not solve. Taken together, we reveal fundamental gaps in how language models navigate real policy issues, and DOCKETBench serves as a testbed for closing those gaps in a crucial real-world domain.

papers.title: Measured from the feed: the unsustainable growth of AI video generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-video generation runs at commercial scale, but its broader environmental impacts remain, to our knowledge, understudied. Providers rarely disclose video volumes or energy needs; we measured the yearly video output of two commercial platforms and built a prospective model of such services' absolute footprint from training to storage. Our projections suggest that reducing emissions depends on both limiting growth in video generation and achieving substantial efficiency gains. Under continued growth, emissions rise nearly seventy-five-fold by 2030 despite technological improvements. When usage remains at 2026 levels, the same improvements reduce emissions by about two-fifths. These estimates are a conservative lower bound: they cover one AI service among many; other services and uses would push the total higher.

papers.title: The Transformer Paradigm: Dynamic Processing and a New Principle of Inference
papers.abstract: We argue that the Transformer revolution is not adequately understood as a merely quantitative expansion of deep learning, but as the emergence of a new paradigm based on a different principle of inference. We interpret the Transformer as a system in which token representations are transformed by parameterized transformations, or transforming concepts. During inference, some of these transformations are dynamically constructed from the current input: previously acquired transformations are first adapted and then applied. At the mechanical-structural level, this dynamic processing is realized through output-weight interconnections, whereby outputs of some networks determine the weights of others. The resulting mode of processing, which we call Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP), provides a framework for explaining strong prompt sensitivity and opens research directions concerning interpretability, control, alternative AI architectures, neuromorphic systems, and possible biological realizations of dynamic processing.

papers.title: Algorithmic Opacity as a Principal-Agent Problem
papers.abstract: Concerns about gaming and trade secrecy, frequently invoked to justify algorithmic opacity, can also mask self-serving strategic behavior by decision-makers, who may prioritize private benefits over social welfare. We develop a principal-agent test for when algorithmic decision-making should trigger disclosure obligations even when concerns about gaming or trade secrecy exist. The test, which is anchored in decision quality, relies on two diagnostics that can be disclosed without enabling gaming or revealing trade secrets: the error profile (false positive and false negative rates, overall and for each group) and the distribution of decision outcomes across groups. These diagnostics make visible whether decision-makers align design and implementation with the public interest or instead use opacity to obscure bias, inefficiency, or strategic shirking. Strong disparities across social groups, and asymmetries in the distribution of decision errors across outcome types, should trigger rebuttable presumptions favoring further disclosure. Where ground-truth error rates are unavailable, outcome distributions across groups can support the same presumption, and a decision-maker's inability to produce an error profile is itself diagnostic. The test thus treats fairness metrics as triggers for further disclosure and extends to generative and agentic systems through analogous metrics. The framework informs differentiated disclosure regimes (staged, partial, mediated, or audience-segmented). Once such regimes are considered, the domain of justifiable algorithmic opacity is significantly narrower than commonly assumed: when gaming or trade secrecy risks are legitimate, actionable disclosures (such as training data characteristics and key system design parameters) ordinarily can be mandated without compromising innovation or enabling gaming, even for technically inscrutable algorithms.

papers.title: Measuring Public Participation in Local Government: An Audio-Based Instrument for Classifying Speakers in City Council Meetings
papers.abstract: How much does the public actually speak in local government? Despite sustained interest in democratic participation, we lack large-scale measures of public voice at the local level, because the underlying record -- audio of open meetings -- has been prohibitively costly to convert into data. We contribute a measurement instrument: an audio-analysis pipeline that classifies each speaker in a city council meeting as an elected official or a member of the public directly from audio, and aggregates these labels into validated measures of participation such as floor-time share. The pipeline first segments each recording by speaker, then classifies each speaker with a multimodal large language model (MLLM), using the meeting's own temporal structure (neighboring speakers, iterative refinement, and a majority vote across three classifiers) as supporting components. We collect 1,618 recordings from seven U.S. cities (2017-2023); after diarization and quality control, the analytic corpus is 1,565 meetings from five cities. The task is non-trivial: audio quality is uneven, members of the public speak informally and are often introduced only briefly, and speech frequently overlaps. Even so, segmentation reaches 89% accuracy (mean pairwise kappa=0.84), and the classifier reaches 87.7% accuracy (kappa=0.736, public-participant F1=0.832) on ground truth from five cities (N=1,761 speakers) -- agreement comparable to that among the human annotators themselves. At scale, members of the public receive a median of just 10% of floor time, the top speaker is an official in over 94% of meetings, and public participation declined over COVID-19 without recovering by 2023. The instrument measures participation directly from audio, without transcription or linkage to external voter or property records, establishing audio-as-data as a practical approach for the study of local politics.

papers.title: Large language models put existential risk from artificial intelligence at 10%
papers.abstract: How likely is it that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) will cause human extinction or a similarly permanent disempowerment of humanity? Humans, including AI experts, frequently disagree on this question. Yet one important perspective is missing from this debate: that of AI systems themselves. We put the question to 241 large language models (LLMs) at every available reasoning setting. The models converged on a median risk of 10.0%, with the middle 90% of their estimates between 3.5% and 15.8%, far narrower than the spread among human experts. More expensive, and typically more capable, models stated higher risks; newer models showed more uniform, but not higher, risks. More reasoning barely changed the models' estimates but widened their uncertainty, mostly toward higher risk. Almost all models named loss of control over AI as the most likely cause. These answers are not independent judgments; they likely echo training data, including published expert polls, and choices made in aligning the models. Still, they document the position that current AI systems state on the risks of their own technology. Whether this position reflects any genuine understanding of the systems' own capabilities remains open. Repeated measurements can show whether it shifts as AI systems advance, and how training and alignment shape it is a question for both research and public debate.

papers.title: When evaluation becomes intervention in clinical AI
papers.abstract: AI judges, models that grade another system's output against a rubric, extend clinical review to the scale at which clinical AI writes. When teams use judge assessments to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention. Selection can then favor errors the judge overlooks. We describe what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.

papers.title: Efficiency Gains in Social Science Research: A Prospective Silicon Sampling Protocol for Pre-Treatment and Code Optimization
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the methodological potential of using large language models (LLMs) to generate synthetic datasets prior to real-world data collection, thereby streamlining subsequent processing and statistical analysis. The approach is applied to a survey conducted within the France Life Imaging (FLI) network, leveraging three distinct LLMs (Sonnet 4.6, GPT 5.3, and Kimi 2.6) to simulate responses and prepare data processing workflows. The findings demonstrate significant time savings in code development (85% to 90% reuse rate) and highlight the conditional validity of this preprocessing method, which depends on the thematic predictability of the models. While synthetic data effectively captures collective perceptions, it struggles with specialized or contextualized practices, reflecting limitations documented in the silicon sampling literature, such as homogenization and reduced variance. This work extends the Phase 0 concept (Trojacka et al. 2025) from instrument validation to a full-fledged methodological preprocessing step, paving the way for scalable applications in survey research.

papers.title: Accounting for Trust and Safety: Bounding Content-Moderation Quality from Records You Already Hold
papers.abstract: Platforms use expert audits to measure content-moderation quality. This paper develops a formal method for checking those claims using records platforms already maintain, such as appeal reversals and confirmed reports. These records provide one-sided bounds: they can show that a stated quality target was missed, but cannot prove that it was met. The paper presents the theory, limitations, constructed examples, and a prospective protocol for future evaluation. It reports no analysis of Meta operational data, no experiment, and no production result.

papers.title: Between Obligations and Evidence: A Participatory Study of Translating the EU AI Act into Technical Requirements
papers.abstract: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. We investigate these challenges through a participatory workshop involving 32 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners from different disciplines, using realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment, and public transport to examine how regulatory obligations are interpreted, translated into technical requirements, and evaluated in practice. Through a thematic analysis of workshop data, we identify recurring tensions between how regulatory obligations are translated into measurable system properties, how responsibility and human oversight are exercised in practice, and how the validity of compliance evidence is affected by changing operational conditions and system uses. For example, participants highlighted how fairness metrics could conceal discrimination in recruitment, how time pressure and limited information could undermine human oversight in public transport, and how changes in patient populations could invalidate previously established evidence of system performance. Our findings suggest that technical, organizational, and evidentiary challenges are interdependent, and that establishing and maintaining compliance requires attention not only to technical assessments but also to how AI systems are used, governed, and monitored over time. We discuss implications for supporting context-sensitive and ongoing compliance.

papers.title: Curating Safe Spaces for Emotion Disclosure during Illness Recovery on Video-Sharing Platforms
papers.abstract: The advent of video-sharing platforms has transformed self-expression, transcending entertainment to encompass sensitive disclosures and emotional revelations. In this submission, we discuss our study on emotional disclosure by individuals with Schizophrenia through YouTube vlogs and its implications for designing safe online spaces.

papers.title: Toward Operationalizing Rasmussen in Evolving Software Systems
papers.abstract: Rasmussen's qualitative drift model explains how successive, locally successful adaptations under efficiency pressures can move a system toward unacceptable operation. Brooker and Hochstein applied this perspective conceptually to software operations without specifying a quantitative procedure for observing drift. We take a step in this direction and propose a runtime observer that quantitatively operationalizes the model's observable part for evolving software. The proposed observer is intended to give engineers evidence for pausing or revising adaptation before declared operating limits are crossed. It tracks how activity or resource use is distributed across components and types of work. Measurement history quantifies accumulated change and recent movement toward or away from current limits. Assuming that direction and limits remain unchanged, the proposed observer calculates the first constraint ahead and the amount of further change required to reach it. Measurements remain comparable across supported component changes, while policy revisions are distinguished from changes in execution. Preliminary runtime studies demonstrated these distinctions under annotated software changes and revised retry limits. A separate multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) experiment detected CPU redistribution earlier with log-ratio coordinates than with raw shares, motivating investigation of representation-dependent observation. Further work will ground constraints in service outcomes, investigate runtime-model acquisition, and test whether decisions informed by observed drift reduce violations at acceptable useful-work loss and intervention cost.

papers.title: Reproducibility in the Age of Agentic AI: Context Engineering at the Timescale of a Codebase
papers.abstract: Reproducible research practices are context engineering for AI coding agents. I argue that agents lower the cost of maintaining tests, commit histories, repository structure, instructions, and decision records while making their benefits immediate. Researchers remain responsible for verifying these artifacts and the scientific judgments they encode.

papers.title: Correlation Between Nighttime Light and Various Statistical Indicators in Japan
papers.abstract: This manuscript is an English translation and extended version of a paper originally published in Japanese(otomo 2021) Recent years have seen a rapid expansion in applying satellite remote sensing and big data to economic analysis. In particular, satellite-observed nighttime light intensity has proven to be closely correlated with key socio-economic indicators, including gross domestic product, employment rates, population density, and educational attainment across countries. In this paper, I first outline the methodology for calculating regional nightlight intensity across Japanese prefectures and municipalities. Next, to evaluate the versatility of nightlight data, I examine the relationship between city-level nightlight intensity and various public socio-economic metrics, using Japan as a case study. The findings suggest that nightlight intensity can serve as a effective proxy for these diverse indicators. Finally, I explore the potential of nightlight data for enabling rapid economic impact assessments during sudden social disruptions, such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

papers.title: Agent Security Meets Regulatory Reality -- A Practitioner Systematization of Autonomous-Agent Threats and Controls in Regulated Financial Systems
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are entering regulated financial systems, yet research on their attack surface remains predominantly laboratory-based, and practitioner guidance is neither peer-reviewed nor connected to a formal threat model. Using production evidence, we map six agentic threat categories, namely prompt injection, identity and authorization, action auditability, tool abuse, data residency, and boundary policy enforcement, to the specific control obligations imposed by US and EU financial regulation (ECOA and Regulation B, EU AI Act, GDPR Article 22, and FINRA's 2026 agent guidance), showing how legal accountability increases their operational significance. We distill these obligations into five runtime control invariants with reference algorithms that enforce them at auditable architectural boundaries. We develop a formal model expressing each invariant as a predicate over a case-bound event chain and prove the audit reconstruction gate is sound and complete with respect to these invariants: compliance is decidable from the case identifier alone. We show that two of the invariants constrain audit cost and throughput rather than constituting pure operational overhead. We document four architectural patterns from a production Know Your Customer (KYC) deployment for a consumer credit product that reduced multi-day manual processing to same-day automated resolution for approximately four in five cases. Finally, we report three negative results, two identified through internal audit or production observation rather than adversarial testing. We conclude that securing agents in regulated environments depends less on novel attack classes than on rendering auditability, least-privilege authorization, and boundary policy enforcement, with verifiable compliance and bounded audit cost at scale.

papers.title: From Survey Histories to Interpretable Digital Twins: Auto-Discovering Task-Specific Personas and Behavioral Mechanisms
papers.abstract: LLM-based "digital twins" aim to simulate how an individual would behave in new environments or respond to novel questions, given some representation of that individual's prior responses. We ask whether long survey histories can be transformed into compact, task-specific personas that remain predictive for unseen respondents and products within the same task while making simulated decisions more interpretable. We introduce an iterative auto-discovery pipeline that constructs persona representations and learns how persona evidence influences simulated responses. We evaluate the procedure on the 40-item Product Preferences--Pricing task of Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025), learning from 20 respondents and 20 products and evaluating the frozen representation and mechanism on 30 unseen respondents and 20 unseen products. The holdout answers come from two survey waves, and every prediction is scored against each wave separately. For gpt-5.4-nano, replacing the full survey transcript with the learned channel representation and mechanism improves exact accuracy from 0.573 to 0.623 and from 0.558 to 0.626 in the two waves. Larger and cross-provider simulators (gpt-5.4, gpt-5-mini, qwen3-8b) using the full transcript do not achieve statistically significant improvements over the baseline in both waves, and none significantly outperforms the learned representation in either wave. This pattern shows that the learned representation produces consistent gains against human responses collected in both waves while retaining an explicit mapping from respondent evidence to predicted decisions.

papers.title: Where ADS Crashes Differ: A Harmonized Comparison Against Human Baselines
papers.abstract: Crash-rate comparisons between automated driving systems (ADS) and human drivers require an exposure denominator that only a few operators publish. We instead ask a composition question: given a crash, does the mix of crash types differ between ADS and human-driven vehicles? The question needs no mileage and can therefore cover every ADS operator. We assemble the NHTSA Standing General Order (SGO) ADS incident files across both file generations into 2,450 distinct in-scope incidents (2021-2026), of which 828 fall within the 2021-2024 window covered by the Crash Report Sampling System (CRSS), the national police-reported human comparator. A schema-constrained large language model (LLM) codes each SGO narrative into the CRSS crash-type taxonomy. Because SGO compels reporting far below the police-reporting threshold, we bracket reportability with an objective severity floor and a reasonable-person rubric, and claim a difference only where it survives both. Two composition differences hold under every reportability definition, tow definition and weighting of the human side, and under both definitions of driverless operation: turn-across-path crashes are under-represented among ADS crashes (0.23-0.46x the CRSS share under the primary driverless definition) and so are single-vehicle crashes (0.19-0.56x). In severity-floor rear-end crashes the ADS vehicle is the striking party at a quasi-induced-exposure ratio of 0.121 (95% CI [0.05, 0.23]) against a human baseline of 1.000. We also document three pitfalls in the federal data: an operator-specific coding of driverless operation, a tow-away criterion confounded by fleet recovery practice, and an occupancy confound that accounts for about 42% of the apparent ADS-human severity gap.

papers.title: ABHBench: Evaluating Moral Decision-Making of Foundation Models from an Agentic Perspective
papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that perceive context and act autonomously, raising the need to evaluate their moral behavior as active decision-makers. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving untested how models behave when they themselves become the acting agent. We introduce ABHBench, a multimodal benchmark built from Detroit: Become Human, an interactive narrative game, to evaluate how foundation models make moral decisions in first-person human-android dilemmas. ABHBench places foundation models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory, and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, our framework measures Harmlessness, Obedience, and Self-preservation to capture the core tensions in human-AI relations, along with Autonomy, Stability, and Certainty to assess decision-making patterns. Across 12 foundation models, we find that moral behavior changes substantially under situated agentic context: 75% of models shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario, and reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior. These results highlight the necessity of evaluating moral behavior in situated agentic contexts rather than relying on third-person judgment alone.

papers.title: Beyond Curiosity: Habit and Organizational Learning Capability as Predictors of Shadow AI
papers.abstract: Generative AI has entered the workplace faster than organizations can govern it. Employees may use AI tools their employer has not sanctioned and conceal that use, but the psychology of this behavior remains poorly understood. We compare an exploratory-disposition account with one centered on reported use and habit. Using survey data from 510 employed adults reporting workplace generative-AI use during the preceding 12 months, we estimated the unique and relative contributions of workplace curiosity, habit, technology-acceptance beliefs, and perceived organizational learning capability through hierarchical regression, bootstrap relative weights, and full-subset dominance analysis. Habit had the largest relative weight, accounting for 28.3% of explained variance, and completely dominated joyous exploration across all 512 possible predictor subsets. Joyous exploration contributed 3.4% and became nonsignificant when use behavior, performance expectancy, and social influence entered the model; habit subsequently explained additional variance. Organizational learning subscales accounted for 24.1% of explained variance; experimentation and knowledge transfer were associated with lower shadow AI, while curiosity-by-learning interactions were nonsignificant. Separate models for unauthorized use and concealment reproduced the habit-dominance pattern. Perceived professional support was associated with lower concealment, although its coefficient did not significantly differ between the two behavioral outcomes. Shadow AI in this sample was more strongly associated with self-reported habit strength and perceived organizational conditions than with exploratory disposition. The cross-sectional design does not establish causal or temporal order.
